title: HSBC turns to 'embedded AI' to counter business-focused fintechs
excerpt: Artificial Intelligence. HSBC turns to 'embedded AI' to counter business-focused fintechs. By John Adams. About John. twitter. johnhadams. mailto. john. adams@arizent. com. linkedin. john-adams-83444310. Published October 20, 2026, 1:59 p. m. EDT. 4 Min Read. Facebook. Twitter. LinkedIn. Email. Key insight : HSBC has developed a set of tools designed to attract business clients to new forms of AI. Forward look : The bank plans to add functions, such as an advanced digital assistant for corporate clients, in the coming months. With banks battling fintechs and each other to sell artificial intelligence-powered financial services, HSBC is stepping up its AI-based offerings to businesses. Processing Content. "What we're hearing most is they want to use AI to pull data from multiple sources in a faster way that allows them to take action," Amber Henderson-Smart, global head of client connectivity for HSBC , told American Banker. HSBC , which is in the midst of a multi-year global initiative to deploy new forms of AI for both internal and external uses , is targeting current and potential business banking clients by making it easier for these businesses to tap machine learning. "The use of AI has been a big foundation for us," Henderson-Smart said. "We want to deliver something suitable for all of the clients that we bank with. ". HSBCnio. The bank's AI service, called HSBCnio, combines financial services, data and analytics with businesses' workflows, with AI or other forms of digital connection available. The bank has redesigned its business banking user interface in an effort to make it easier for businesses to view cash positions, payments, loans and foreign exchange transactions. AI access is supported through HSBC's Model Context Protocol, which enables clients' own AI tools to query authorized account and transaction information, helping human workers find and interpret banking data. The Model Context Protocol is an open standard created by Anthropic that lets AI applications connect to external systems such as databases, files and APIs. For HSBC , the MCP works with the bank's APIs, SDKs and sandbox, enabling treasury and finance teams to embed banking data into their internal platforms. "There's less effort required for where they are connecting to AI," Henderson-Smart said. HSBC plans to add more banking products and AI-enabled products to HSBCnio over time, including "Ask HSB," an AI-enabled feature designed to help clients query and interpret their banking information. In business. HSBC does not release the number of business clients it has, but says it has about 41 million global consumer and business customers in 56 countries. The bank's corporate customers include a range of multinational corporations, small to mid-sized businesses, government and public sector entities and other financial institutions. HSBCnio follows earlier AI-related moves at HSBC , including a global AI center in Singapore, support for agentic treasury products, AI-enable digital payments, and other work in natural-language processing, data science and AI governance. It also partners with Google to analyze about 1. 35 billion transactions per month across about 40 million accounts, with HSBC reporting this system identifies two to four times more financial crime than human-based methods while reducing false positives by 60%. The bank has also said the AI-driven strategy could eventually reduce HSBC's workforce by about 10%. There's also a competitive impetus for the bank. HSBC's business-focused AI product comes as banks , payment fintechs , and card networks invest in new forms of AI, as well as technology that enables access to AI and manages security risk. The launch follows a proof of concept announced earlier this year and means LHV’s retail customers can now get immediate answers to everyday banking questions by email, around the clock. The AI agent handles common enquiries from start to finish, such as what to do about a lost card, an explanation of a payment, transfer queries, or what happens next with an existing request. Cases that are sensitive, complex or outside the agent’s approved procedures are passed to LHV’s customer support team. Faster answers, more time for complex cases. Like other banks, LHV Bank's traditional queue-based approach to customer queries didn't distinguish between simple questions and complex ones. With this launch, simple queries get immediate answers, freeing up LHV's team to focus on the cases where human judgement matters most. How it works. AI agent handles scoped journeys: Using Gradient Labs, LHV Bank's AI agent resolves clearly defined customer journeys from start to finish. Works within set limits: The agent operates only within approved procedures, tools and controls. Humans set the rules: LHV's teams define each process, its boundaries and what the agent is allowed to do. Humans approve changes: Any updates are tested and signed off by LHV’s team before going live. Ongoing oversight: LHV monitors quality and handles any exceptions the agent escalates. Guardrails built for regulated banking. As LHV Bank operates in a regulated environment, its AI agent pairs large language models with deterministic guardrails. These control what data and tools the agent can access, when actions are blocked or escalated, and how complaints and vulnerable customers are handled. Customer data is never used to train the models, or build the agent, and is accessed only during live interactions. Improving the agent like software. title: FCA receives 'hundreds' of applications for pair of senior AI leadership roles
excerpt: FCA receives 'hundreds' of applications for pair of senior AI leadership roles. By Jonathan Easton 20/10/2026. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said it has received hundreds of applications for two senior artificial intelligence roles, as the UK regulator develops automated tools to monitor financial crime and supervise thousands of firms. Jessica Rusu, the FCA’s chief data, information and artificial intelligence officer, told Bloomberg at an event in London on Monday that candidates were attracted by the opportunity to tackle “fascinating and interesting problems”, despite potentially higher pay at AI companies. The regulator recently closed applications for a head of agentic AI and data science research and a head of department for AI and technology security operations. The former role offered salaries of £140,000 to £190,000 in London, or £126,000 to £171,000 in Leeds or Edinburgh, with the second position advertised within the same salary range. The recruitment drive forms part of the FCA’s ambition to expand its use of AI while overseeing its adoption across the 35,500 firms under its supervision. Rusu said the watchdog was developing AI tools to monitor anti-money laundering controls at an additional 60,000 firms, as part of a new responsibility that comes into effect in 2028. The regulator is also deploying automated and agentic AI agents to help supervise approximately 9,000 small wholesale market firms that report transaction data. The FCA is encouraging financial services businesses to adopt appropriate safeguards as they introduce AI into their operations. Rusu called on firms to help consumers understand the limitations of financial information and advice generated by AI models through “clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers”. Cybersecurity is another area of focus, with the regulator working with financial services firms on their defences against risks associated with AI. Security concerns surrounding Anthropic’s Mythos model earlier this year have highlighted the challenges facing organisations adopting the technology. “AI is moving faster than any regulatory framework was designed,” Rusu said, adding that regulators would increasingly need to make decisions without precedent while maintaining trust in financial services. The FCA is also confronting a rise in AI-enabled fraud, including deepfake videos promoting fraudulent investment opportunities. Rusu said the regulator would pursue more financial crime investigations if it had unlimited resources, warning that such fraud “really undermines growth”. Share Story:.

The service can resolve common queries relating to lost cards, payments, transfers and existing requests, while more complex or sensitive cases are escalated to the bank’s customer support team. LHV said the technology would allow its staff to focus on enquiries requiring human judgement, rather than processing routine questions through traditional customer service queues. ADVERTISEMENT. The system also uses safeguards to determine which data and tools the agent can access, when actions should be blocked or escalated, and how complaints and vulnerable customers are handled. According to LHV, customer data is accessed only during live interactions and is not used to train AI models or build the agent. The bank is also using Gradient Labs’ Collaborate platform, which allows its operations, product, engineering, risk and compliance teams to develop, test and approve changes to the AI agent before they are introduced. ADVERTISEMENT. Kris Brewster, interim CEO of LHV Bank, said: “As a digital-only bank, we don’t have to accept the way customer service has always been done. Others in the industry are using AI co-pilots that simply draft replies for staff to approve. “This might speed up individual steps, but customer queries still sit in the same queue, and when the AI is usually right, people can start approving suggestions without checking them closely. ADVERTISEMENT. “We wanted to go further and give customers an answer straight away, while keeping our people firmly in control of how the service works and stepping in whenever a case needs them. Getting that balance right is what responsible innovation looks like to us. ”. ADVERTISEMENT. Dimitri Masin, CEO of Gradient Labs, added: “The future of AI in financial services is not a faster human approving AI suggestions at every step. “It is trusted agents taking responsibility for defined work, supported by deterministic controls, clear escalation points and human judgement where it matters. title: Big Banks Won’t Let Outside AI Agents Move Money
excerpt: Big Banks Won’t Let Outside AI Agents Move Money. By PYMNTS | October 19, 2026. |. Highlights. JPMorganChase, Citigroup, Bank of America and Charles Schwab all said in one week that outside AI agents cannot move customer money, with Schwab blocking Meta’s Muse dozens of times a week. The banks still let authorized connectors read balances, and Bank of America is writing liability rules with agent developers while JPMorgan builds its own Smart Cash sweep and Schwab rolls out Charley. PYMNTS Intelligence found that 37% of AI power users already treat AI as their main tool for managing finances and banking, and consumers want an agent to ask permission before it completes a purchase. A customer who hands a login to an artificial intelligence agent now gets turned away at four of the biggest names in banking in the United States. Charles Schwab sees the attempts firsthand. Across all its clients, the brokerage blocks the big, unauthorized AI agents , including Meta ’s Muse , “in the tens and 20s” each week, CEO Rick Wurster said, Bloomberg reported Friday (Oct. 16). JPMorganChase CEO Jamie Dimon warned of “ rogue agents ” and said outside agents would not get inside the bank during a third-quarter earnings call Tuesday (Oct. 13), PYMNTS reported. Bank of America followed a day later with a condition rather than a ban. The bank is limiting agents’ access to consumer deposits while it writes protocols that decide which party is liable for a payment an AI authorizes, and CEO Brian Moynihan said Wednesday (Oct. 14) that a human should stay in the loop to approve money moving out of an account, the Financial Times reported Friday. By Friday, Citigroup had drawn the same line. The bank does not let third-party agents log into accounts or transact, the FT report said. Agents Can See Accounts but Cannot Pay From Them. All four firms kept the read-only door open while closing the one that moves money. At JPMorganChase, outside agents can see balances when a customer authorizes a connector such as Plaid , but they cannot send money or pay bills, and the bank gave no timeline for changing that, the PYMNTS report said. Dimon told analysts on the same call that customers who use outside agents should understand “the liability transfer. ”. Citi lets certain authorized open banking providers retrieve account information in read-only form, according to the FT report. Schwab will build model context protocol servers so a client’s chosen AI model can check balances and run research under rules Schwab sets, Wurster said in the Bloomberg report. “We’re not going to allow them to move money…,” he said, per the report. Bank of America is working with AI agent developers on protocols governing how an agent may interact with a customer account, so that customers do not find money has left an account without understanding why or where it went, the FT report said. Moynihan said during a Wednesday earnings call that he does not expect agents to pull deposits from the bank, PYMNTS reported. Customers hold checking balances to pay bills rather than to earn yield, and that excess liquidity is already directed to the bank’s yield products. Banks Keep the Money-Moving Job for Their Own Assistants. The transfers the banks will not hand to an outside agent are the ones they plan to run themselves. Dimon wrote in his 2025 shareholder letter that JPMorgan’s Smart Cash capability would move client money automatically between checking accounts and higher-yielding brokerage products in 2026, PYMNTS reported Oct. 8. title: How banks are expanding AI while restricting outside agents
excerpt: Banks are expanding AI use while controlling access. A bank can deploy AI for employees and customers while restricting access by outside AI agents. JPMorgan Chase is doing both, separating its decision to use the technology from its decision to admit external systems. For banking technology leaders, that separation raises three practical questions: which uses deserve permission, which models justify their cost and which work the bank should do itself. Banks addressed those questions in earnings discussions about agentic AI, systems that can carry out tasks, and AI’s operating benefits and costs. JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo discussed their approaches on Tuesday’s Q3 2026 calls, followed by Bank of America on Wednesday. Their decisions cover access for outside agents, model routing, the assignment of a query to a particular AI model, and in-sourcing, which means bringing work inside the organization. Each changes a different part of how a bank deploys AI. Outside agents face separate access decisions. Access comes first because an outside agent needs permission to operate within a bank’s systems. JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon described the bank as neither “against agents or for agents,” pointing to its adoption for employees and customers. Dimon has a commercial interest in gaining AI’s benefits while protecting customers and the business from its risks. His position separates the value of using agents from the exposure created by admitting them. Dimon explained the security concern: “because you don’t want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them. ” Thousands describes the possible scale of rogue-agent activity. As the number of agents grows, the bank could face many sources of unwanted activity, making control over entry an important part of deployment. JPMorgan is therefore developing tools to protect customers while restricting access to its systems. “ We ’re not going to allow just any outside agent to come inside the company because that’s just too risky,” Dimon said. A provider whose agent is refused entry cannot run it inside the bank, even as JPMorgan expands its own AI use. Wells Fargo described how it would assess third-party technology by weighing its benefits against its risks. CEO Charlie Scharf said the bank saw opportunities for itself and its customers while “taking a disciplined approach to managing risk. ” Scharf also has a commercial interest in finding useful capabilities for Wells Fargo’s customers while limiting the bank’s exposure. Scharf set out what that assessment would cover: “ We will also evaluate how third-party models and agents can provide value-added capabilities to our clients, while at the same time considering the potential risk these tools can introduce for both our clients and Wells Fargo,” he said. A capability can help a client while creating exposure for the institution providing it, so the assessment covers both parties. Wells Fargo described an evaluation process; JPMorgan stated a restriction on entry. The statements establish different approaches to access. LET'S TALK!. A project in mind? After a bank approves an AI use, it still has to decide which model should handle the work. JPMorgan is pursuing a model-agnostic strategy, meaning it aims to avoid dependence on a single model, to preserve its ability to switch providers and manage spending. Dimon pointed to routing tools that direct queries toward the quickest, cheapest models. By choosing a model as work is assigned, the bank can manage costs query by query. Routing works when the model fits the request, because different queries make different demands on a system. “You don’t need the most expensive thing for every query you have and very often people just see the one they’re comfortable with,” Dimon said. To get there, the bank is taking a deeper, strategic look across workflows with transformation in mind. Shafiq, head of AI products and solutions at Wells, joined the bank in February to oversee the roadmap and development of AI-powered products to be used across the company. He was previously a leader at Amazon Web Services. “The year started off by making sure that we have the right tools enabled for our employees,” Shafiq said in an interview. From there, Wells began to identify targeted uses and is seeing tangible benefits from those. In 2027, rethinking workflows and integrating AI into those is “the biggest area of focus” for Shafiq. “That is something I'm going to spend a lot more time and energy on [in] the remainder of the year, as well as next year,” he said. The $2. 3 trillion-asset bank’s effort to derive value from AI goes beyond the application of a single tool or focusing on a few use cases, he said. “Our goal here is to use AI to fundamentally transform how our bank operates,” Shafiq said. Shafiq, speaking Tuesday at the Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas, said San Francisco-based Wells Fargo sees four core components to achieving that goal:. Hub-and-spoke model. That means one central team at Wells works on elements of AI integration that affect the entire bank, delivered by teams that own the specific applications, he said. “Governance, security, controls, prioritization – all of that is centrally controlled because one team can build that out more efficiently, and then everyone can use it,” he said. And the spoke element is crucial, because “domain expertise is what will matter a lot. ”. Focus on highest impact uses. “Every project, every initiative suddenly has become AI, or AI-enabled, or AI-first, or AI-native, depending on the definition,” he said. To zero in on applications that will move the needle, Wells is emphasizing effort and attention on highest impact uses, he said. “There's going to be a disproportionate amount of value being created by a small number of use cases, and so we want to make sure that we're working on the right use cases, and we're not stretched thin or boiling the ocean,” he said. Speed with discipline. “The pace of change is remarkable, and so we do want to have a faster operating model, but not at the expense of safety, control, guardrails, governance,” he said. That means enabling the right controls, establishing an appropriate governance framework and having risk conversations at the outset. The bank’s approach “doesn't mean that we're not going to move fast. It just simply means that we're going to move fast with the appropriate guardrails,” he said. The bank may be highly regulated, but Shafiq said Wells has shifted the conversation – instead of “we can’t do that,” the approach is, “what do we need to do to do this safely, effectively?”. Upskill and enable the workforce. Wells strives to empower its 197,000 employees across the company to tap AI tools to “become superhuman,” he said. “Having structured learning, training, development is super key. ” At Wells’ size, driving adoption may take a bit longer, he noted. title: World Bank launches first digital strategy to expand access, jobs, AI readiness
excerpt: . Spread the word. The World Bank Group has launched its first digital strategy, pooling its public and private sector capabilities to help developing countries expand affordable digital access, improve services, and create jobs. The strategy rests on four priorities: expanding connectivity; making devices and data more affordable; strengthening digital services and skills; and building the foundations for artificial intelligence. “Digital technology can help countries create jobs and make scarce resources go further. Realizing that potential requires a comprehensive approach—from reliable connectivity and affordable devices to digital skills and useful services,” said World Bank Group President Ajay Banga. “Our first digital strategy brings these pieces together, helping countries build the foundations to benefit from today’s digital tools and the promise of small AI—AI for the people. ”. The launch comes as developing countries grapple with limited resources and a growing need for jobs. Over the next 10 to 15 years, 1. 2 billion young people will reach working age in these countries, while their economies are projected to create only about 420 million jobs. Barriers remain steep. Over 2 billion people were offline globally in 2025. Only 23 percent of people in low-income countries used the internet, against 94 percent in high-income countries. Many people live within network coverage but cannot afford a smartphone or data, lack digital skills, or have little access to relevant services. On connectivity, the Bank will help close gaps from international cables to networks serving homes, schools, and clinics, supporting shared infrastructure, encouraging competition, and using public finance and guarantees to draw private investment into underserved markets. Where electricity and connectivity are both missing, the strategy backs planning them together. On affordability, it supports efforts to lower the cost of entry-level smartphones and broadband, through partnerships with manufacturers, mobile operators, financial institutions, and refurbishment businesses, including options for paying over time. On services and skills, the Bank will back digital identification, payments, and secure information-sharing systems, alongside digital literacy and training linked to employment. On AI, the strategy stresses “small AI”: tools adapted to specific tasks and local conditions, such as helping farmers identify crop disease, supporting health workers, or helping businesses manage inventory. Safeguards covering privacy, cybersecurity, and fraud protection run across all four priorities. The Bank also announced the AI Infrastructure and Readiness Initiative, which aims to give governments in emerging markets access to affordable computing capacity through shared, pay-as-you-go GPU infrastructure, as an alternative to standalone national data centres. It will focus initially on Africa and Latin America, with Cassava Technologies and NVIDIA as knowledge partners. Spread the word. AI. Job. World Bank.

Announced in Seoul on Tuesday, the strategy brings together the institution’s public and private sector capabilities to help developing economies expand digital connectivity, improve access to technology and create employment opportunities. World Bank Group President Ajay Banga said the initiative would focus on practical applications of technology, particularly affordable AI tools that can improve productivity and public services. “Digital technology can help countries create jobs and make scarce resources go further. Realizing that potential requires a comprehensive approach—from reliable connectivity and affordable devices to digital skills and useful services,” Banga said. “Our first digital strategy brings these pieces together, helping countries build the foundations to benefit from today’s digital tools and the promise of small AI—AI for the people,” he added. The announcement comes amid a growing employment challenge across developing economies, where millions of young people are expected to enter the labour market in the coming years. According to the World Bank, approximately 1. 2 billion young people will reach working age over the next 10 to 15 years, while their economies are projected to generate only about 420 million jobs. The strategy identifies digital technology as a means of boosting productivity and expanding employment opportunities across sectors such as infrastructure, energy, agriculture, healthcare, tourism and manufacturing. Under the strategy, the World Bank will support investments in international cables, national broadband networks and local connectivity infrastructure serving homes, businesses, schools and healthcare facilities. It will also work with manufacturers, mobile operators and financial institutions to reduce the cost of entry-level smartphones and broadband services. title: World Bank Launches Digital Strategy and AI Compute Initiative
excerpt: . Back to News / Technology. Build your reading streak 0 / 3 today · Counts at 25%. The World Bank Group publicly launched its first digital strategy on October 20, linking broadband, affordable devices, public services and AI readiness to a shared-compute initiative initially focused on Africa and Latin America. The announcement in Seoul brings the Bank’s public-sector finance and policy work together with private investment and guarantees. A 2025 Nigeria project appraisal had already referred to a WBG Digital Strategy (2025), which it said was discussed by the Board on July 24, 2025. The October event is its public launch, not necessarily the start of development. A related AI Infrastructure and Readiness Initiative would help emerging-market governments access shared, pay-as-you-go GPU capacity. The October 20 announcement did not specify participating countries, sites, capacity, pricing or a funding envelope. Four foundations before AI scale. The plan treats AI readiness as one part of a wider digital system, not a stand-alone model-building programme. Its four priorities are:. Connectivity: extend reliable networks from international links and national backbones to homes, schools, clinics and businesses. Affordability: reduce barriers to smartphones and data, including through competition, financing and refurbished devices. Services and skills: strengthen digital identity, payments, secure data-sharing, literacy and job-linked training. AI readiness: improve access to computing, usable local data and skills, while supporting practical tools adapted to specific tasks and local conditions. Privacy, cybersecurity and fraud safeguards run across all four areas. The strategy combines finance, guarantees, policy advice and private investment around country priorities; it is a framework for future work, not a list of loans or a promise every government will receive a project. The divide is more than network coverage. The latest International Telecommunication Union estimates show why connectivity cannot be measured only by whether a signal reaches a village. About 6 billion people were online in 2025, while more than a quarter of the world’s population remained offline. Internet use reached 94 per cent in high-income countries and 23 per cent in low-income countries; the ITU’s regional estimate for Africa was 36 per cent. The World Bank says many people are within network coverage but still cannot afford a suitable phone or data, lack digital skills, or have few useful services available in a language and format they can use. That distinction matters: new fibre and towers may be necessary, but do not alone resolve device prices, unreliable electricity, digital literacy or the cost of online services. The jobs argument is central to the announcement. The Bank projects 1. 2 billion young people in developing countries will reach working age over the next 10 to 15 years, while about 420 million jobs are projected to be created. It says digital tools could help firms reach customers, improve productivity and access finance, and lower the cost of public services. These are intended growth channels, not a measured estimate of jobs this strategy will produce. What the shared-compute initiative does—and does not say. GPU infrastructure supplies specialized processors used to develop or run AI applications. The Bank describes a shared, pay-as-you-go model as an alternative to each country building its own data centre. The initial geographic focus is Africa and Latin America, and the announcement names Cassava Technologies and NVIDIA as knowledge partners. The announcement does not say NVIDIA has committed chips, Cassava will build a facility, or governments have received grants or compute credits.
